title: Integrating Generative AI in Knowledge Building
extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can be integrated into K-12 learning in ways that support both disciplinary learning and AI literacy. The authors argue that although there is growing interest in AI literacy and in using AI for learning, there is little empirical research on the actual processes by which students use GenAI in classroom learning. The study therefore asks two questions: how high school students incorporated ChatGPT into knowledge-building work, and how their AI literacy developed through that process.

The intervention was a teacher-designed integration of ChatGPT into a high school World Religions course structured around Knowledge Building pedagogy. Across roughly two phases of classroom activity, students used ChatGPT first to explore the problem space by critiquing AI-generated essays and generating inquiry questions, and later to deepen inquiry through guided conversations with ChatGPT, fact-checking, peer discussion, and collaborative posting in Knowledge Forum. The teacher explicitly scaffolded use through class discussions, prompts, a steering prompt for ChatGPT interaction, expectations for fact-checking, and requirements to document and cite AI use. The instructional model was teacher-led and classroom-based, with collaborative small-group work and individual use of ChatGPT embedded in ongoing inquiry and writing.

The study took place with 10 consented high school students and one teacher in a K-12 setting in a major South American city. Students came from three different schools and were enrolled in an elective course conducted in English. Data consisted primarily of end-of-semester semi-structured student interviews, supplemented by classroom artifacts from Miro and Knowledge Forum and teacher planning/reflection documents. The analysis used qualitative coding focused on students' uses of ChatGPT and dimensions of AI literacy.

The main conclusions are that students used ChatGPT in multiple ways: for information search, brainstorming, generating questions, supporting writing, summarizing, and keeping up with discussion. Students also developed emerging AI literacy, including awareness of strengths, weaknesses, risks, and some mechanisms of ChatGPT, though their understanding was often partial and sometimes inaccurate. The paper concludes that GenAI can productively support collaborative knowledge building when educators provide structured pedagogical guidance, opportunities for critique and reflection, and explicit scaffolds for mindful, ethical human-AI partnership rather than simple answer-getting.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample qualitative classroom study using interviews, artifacts, and teacher notes in a real K-12 setting, but it lacks a comparison group, standardized outcome measures, and causal identification. It provides useful implementation and mechanism evidence, meeting only limited credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but unclear impacts: students perceived gains in efficiency, idea generation, and critical AI use, but outcomes were not quantified and academic gains were not directly measured. As a result, overall impact remains modest or uncertain.

interventions.use_case: High school students used ChatGPT as a conversational learning partner within a teacher-designed knowledge building pedagogy to generate inquiry questions, obtain brief explanatory answers with multiple perspectives, receive follow-up questions, support research and discussion, and assist with essay planning and writing in a World Religions course.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative study of 10 high school students in a World Religions course, interviews and classroom artifacts suggested ChatGPT supported domain learning by helping students search for information efficiently, surface diverse perspectives, and keep up with discussions. However, students also reported misinformation, dated content, and difficulty fact-checking convincing outputs, so evidence for improvement in subject-matter learning was process-based rather than tied to measured achievement gains. No standardized achievement outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student interview reports and classroom artifacts about learning support in a World Religions course; no direct achievement test reported

finding.finding_summary: Students described using ChatGPT to support literacy-related tasks including generating essay outlines, revising drafts, summarizing texts, gathering arguments, and correcting minor writing mistakes. Some students viewed it as a useful support for starting and improving writing, whereas others warned that overreliance, copying outputs, and inaccurate content could undermine authentic writing quality and learning; no direct reading or writing performance measures were collected. The paper therefore provides implementation evidence rather than causal evidence on literacy gains.
finding.measure: Student self-reports and artifacts on essay writing, revision, summarization, and writing support; no standardized literacy assessment reported

finding.finding_summary: The study found qualitative evidence that structured ChatGPT use, combined with teacher scaffolds, supported durable skills such as critical evaluation, prompt engineering, fact-checking, metacognitive reflection, collaboration, and configuring an appropriate human-AI partnership. Students described learning to refine prompts, compare outputs against external sources, discuss AI-generated ideas with peers, and set boundaries on use, though these outcomes were not quantified with validated scales. Evidence comes from interviews, Knowledge Forum posts, and teacher scaffolds with n=10 students.
finding.measure: Interview evidence and classroom artifacts concerning critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, prompt engineering, and fact-checking practices

finding.finding_summary: About 70% of interviewed students reported that ChatGPT increased efficiency in information search by allowing natural-language queries, maintaining conversational context, and providing concise answers more quickly than search engines. Students also used it to reduce workload in routine tasks such as outlining essays, summarizing text, and getting quick help during class, although no time-on-task or productivity metrics were formally collected.
finding.measure: Student self-reported efficiency in information search and task completion

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT could increase engagement by making interactions feel personal, helping them participate in class discussions, and sparking interest through idea generation. At the same time, some students voiced concern about dependence, reduced attention span, and passive shortcut use, indicating potential downsides for self-regulation and healthy engagement. These findings are qualitative and based on interviews rather than validated motivation or self-regulation instruments.
finding.measure: Student interview reports about engagement, personal connection, dependence, and self-regulation concerns
